question: Which childhood renal malignancy most commonly presents as a painless, firm, smooth abdominal mass?
cited_learning_objective: Review the clinical features of common genitourinary cancers

options.rationale: Wilms tumor commonly presents in childhood as an incidentally discovered, painless abdominal mass.
Renal cell carcinoma is the common solid renal malignancy of adults; an incidentally detected adult renal mass would support this diagnosis.
Upper tract urothelial carcinoma arises from the lining of the renal drainage system; a filling defect in the renal pelvis would support it.
Bladder urothelial carcinoma most commonly presents with painless gross hematuria; a bladder lesion on cystoscopy would support it.
Prostate cancer primarily affects older men; an elevated prostate-specific antigen or abnormal prostate examination would support it.

question: Which examination is the best diagnostic test for a suspected bladder malignancy?

options.rationale: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging is used to evaluate local extension in prostate cancer; suspected extracapsular or seminal vesicle involvement would support its use.

Urine cytology checks for malignant cells but does not replace direct visualization; it is an adjunct in the bladder cancer workup.
Transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy evaluates suspected prostate cancer; an elevated prostate-specific antigen would support that procedure.

question: Which tumor marker is elevated in most non-seminoma germ cell tumors but not in pure seminoma?

options.rationale: Prostate-specific antigen is used in prostate cancer evaluation; suspected prostatic disease would make this marker relevant.
Erythropoietin can be produced by renal cell carcinoma; accompanying erythrocytosis would support that association.
Parathyroid-related peptide can produce hypercalcemia in renal cell carcinoma; elevated calcium with a renal mass would support it.
β-hCG is elevated in most non-seminomas but can also be elevated in some mixed seminomas, so it does not provide the stated pure-seminoma contrast.
α-Fetoprotein is elevated in the majority of non-seminoma germ cell tumors and is not elevated in pure seminoma.

question: Which metastatic pattern is most characteristic of prostate cancer?
cited_learning_objective: Review the clinical features of common genitourinary cancers

options.rationale: Lytic pelvic lesions are associated with metastatic renal cell carcinoma; a renal primary would make this pattern appropriate.
Bone is the most common blood-borne metastatic site of prostate cancer, which produces an osteoblastic pattern.
Renal vein invasion is characteristic of renal cell carcinoma; a solid renal mass with venous extension would support it.
Superficial bladder involvement describes non-invasive bladder cancer rather than metastatic prostate cancer.
Retroperitoneal lymph-node spread defines stage II testicular cancer; a testicular primary would support this pattern.

question: A renal malignancy produces erythrocytosis through secretion of a tumor-derived mediator. Which mediator is responsible?
cited_learning_objective: Review the clinical features of common genitourinary cancers

options.rationale: Renal cell carcinoma can produce erythropoietin, causing erythrocytosis as a paraneoplastic manifestation.

Prostate-specific antigen is associated with prostate cancer evaluation and does not explain erythrocytosis.
α-Fetoprotein is a testicular tumor marker; a non-seminoma germ cell tumor would make it relevant.

question: A bladder tumor extends into the detrusor layer without described spread into surrounding fat. Which tumor stage applies?

options.rationale: T1 bladder cancer is superficial and non-invasive; confinement above the muscle layer would make this stage correct.
T3 disease extends into or through perivesical fat; documented fat involvement would make this stage correct.
T4b disease invades the pelvic or abdominal wall; such wall invasion would be required for this stage.
T2 bladder cancer is defined by invasion of the muscular layer.
M1 denotes distant metastasis; evidence of a distant tumor deposit would make this designation correct.

question: A young man undergoes orchiectomy for a localized testicular malignancy. Which postoperative finding most strongly indicates residual disease?

options.rationale: AFP normalization within four weeks suggests elimination of localized tumor rather than residual disease.
hCG normalization within two weeks suggests that localized marker-producing tumor has been eliminated.
Failure of tumor markers to normalize after surgery indicates residual testicular cancer.
Persistently negative follow-up markers do not indicate residual marker-producing disease; conversion to positive would suggest recurrence.

question: A renal tumor extends into the inferior vena cava. Which management component specifically addresses this extension?

Ablation is an option for a small renal mass; confinement to a T1 lesion would make it appropriate.

question: Which pairing correctly connects a genitourinary malignancy with its characteristic bone-metastasis pattern?

options.rationale: Prostate cancer commonly spreads to bone and produces osteoblastic metastatic disease.
The depicted prostate cancer pattern is osteoblastic, whereas lytic pelvic lesions are associated with metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
An osteoblastic metastatic pattern is linked to prostate cancer, not presented as the characteristic pattern of bladder cancer.

question: A patient with non-invasive bladder cancer receives an attenuated organism through a urethral catheter. Which effect mediates treatment?

question: Which presentation and mechanism are correctly paired for renal cell carcinoma?

options.text: Scrotal ultrasound rather than transrectal biopsy
options.rationale: A suspected testicular mass is initially evaluated with scrotal ultrasound, whereas prostate cancer evaluation can include transrectal prostate biopsy.

question: Which combination correctly links testicular cancer stage with anatomic extent?

question: A 4-year-old child has an incidentally discovered, painless, smooth abdominal mass. Imaging shows a large right renal mass without distant disease. Which next management approach is most appropriate?

question: A 63-year-old man has lower-limb edema. Contrast imaging shows a solid renal mass extending through the renal vein into a central abdominal vein. Which procedure best addresses the advanced local feature?
